In a joint status report released this morning, Apple said it is still awaiting further documents from Jon Prosser and hopes to re-depose Michael Ramacciotti, with both defendants pushing back on how Apple is handling the case. Details below.

According to the joint status report filed with Judge James Donato, the divide is widening between Apple, leaker Jon Prosser, and Michael Ramacciotti over who bears responsibility for the delays in Apple's trade secrets lawsuit filed against both defendants in July 2025.

A little background

A quick refresher: Apple filed suit shortly after unveiling iOS 26, alleging that Prosser and Ramacciotti had improperly misappropriated trade secrets. The case centers on a video by Prosser in which he leaked portions of the system, including design elements that turned out to be part of the major Liquid Glass visual overhaul.

Apple claims Ramacciotti improperly accessed an employee's developer iPhone, an employee who was subsequently fired over the incident. Ramacciotti also had a FaceTime call with Prosser during which he showed him unreleased iOS features running on that device.

The case has had its share of twists and turns: Prosser had a default judgment entered against him by the clerk for failing to respond to Apple's lawsuit within the deadline, though Prosser has consistently denied ignoring the case.

Eight months later, the court agreed to vacate that default judgment and give him another chance to formally answer the allegations.

Court filings show that the Ramacciotti side has responded to Apple's suit and has largely cooperated with its discovery requests.

But since Prosser retained counsel and formally entered the case, things have shifted, and the three parties are increasingly at odds over who should bear responsibility for the alleged trade secret disclosures and the subsequent delays.

The latest joint status report

Turning to the latest status report, Apple says it wants Ramacciotti to update his written responses and sit for a second deposition to address what it describes as "inconsistencies between his testimony and that of Mr. Prosser."

Ramacciotti, however, says he is willing to sit for another deposition only after Apple provides "a roadmap to resolving the claims against him, including what information Apple still needs from him (if any)."

As for Prosser, Apple says it is "still waiting for him to produce certain additional documents requested more than three months ago," including revenue reports and analytics for his YouTube channel, as well as relevant communications with third parties that he referenced during his deposition.

Prosser immediately pushed back, arguing that "the purported trade secrets at issue no longer appear to be trade secrets, but rather have entered the public domain." In other words, his argument appears to be that because Apple has already released the iOS update featuring Liquid Glass, the core information underlying the lawsuit is now publicly available and therefore no longer meets the definition of a trade secret.

As part of the joint status update, Ramacciotti asked the court to hold a status hearing this month, at which he wants Apple to explain what additional information it still needs from him. He also wants Apple to either drop its claims against him or commit to taking the case to trial within the following 30 days.

Apple, for its part, wants discovery to continue, including a second deposition of Ramacciotti and continued efforts to obtain the documents Prosser has not yet produced. Prosser, meanwhile, argues he has fulfilled the discovery obligations he agreed to and opposes Apple's continuing demands for more materials from him.

If Judge Donato does not grant Ramacciotti's request for a status hearing, the parties have proposed filing another joint status report on December 2.
